title: [Experiment, Analysis, and Benchmark] Batch Fidelity Certificates for Semantic COUNT: Scope and Full Policy Cost
abstract: Putting several rows in one language-model prompt can reduce requests for a semantic filter and COUNT, but checking the batch plan also costs work. We empirically audit an existing current-input fidelity checker by connecting its sampled comparisons to the complete query result and policy bill. The study uses native LOTUS filtering and a declared custom batch operator in 36 configurations over six workloads, two text domains and two models, with 16 additional policies comparing checking budgets. Our joint benefit criterion requires a delivered batch result, at most 5% row disagreement with each of two separate singleton executions, fewer requests and fewer raw input-plus-output tokens. Unchecked random and similarity batches meet it in one and two of the 12 primary configurations, respectively; the checked policy meets it in none. Source COUNT accuracy is a separate outcome. The sole accepted deployment meets observed fidelity tolerance, but calibration turns its token saving into a 3.01% increase, despite 79.69% fewer requests. Raising the budget from 80 to 320 probes leaves every follow-up policy in singleton fallback with a higher bill. All 48 cache-enabled fixed-plan executions use less raw input but more uncached input than their singleton baselines; all 24 cache-disabled executions use less of both. These cache rankings apply to the declared repeated-predicate representation. Distinguishing delivered labels, output format, reference fidelity, source COUNT and complete costs makes the bounded plan decisions reproducible.
keywords: semantic query processing, large language models, COUNT, fidelity certification, prefix caching, query optimization
